claims.text: An integrated machine-learning framework can optimize thermomechanical processing to improve strength and ductility concurrently in multicomponent alloys.
Machine-learning-optimized processing can tailor coherent precipitation microstructures.
Conventionally processed homogeneous or dual-phase alloys typically exhibit a strength–ductility trade-off.
As-cast or cold-rolled states are examples of the proposed conventional initial state.
A data-driven model can identify optimal annealing times, annealing temperatures, and deformation schedules.
Stepwise thermomechanical processing selected by machine learning promotes coherent precipitate architectures.
The proposed method is intended to operate under room-temperature tensile loading and moderate thermal environments.
The tailored coherent precipitates may include lamellar delta phases and gamma-double-prime particles.
The combination of dislocation pinning and planar slip balances strengthening and ductility.
Machine-learning-predicted processing routes can precisely control microstructural evolution.
The proposed approach enables independent tuning of precipitate distribution and morphology.
Controlling precipitate distribution and morphology manages dislocation motion and enhances strength without severely compromising ductility.
The optimized alloy will have higher yield strength and improved ductility than a conventionally processed alloy.
Traditional grain refinement and precipitation hardening typically improve one mechanical property at the expense of the other.
Advanced computational and data-driven design tools are relevant to exploration of high-entropy-alloy composition and temperature spaces.
The specific machine-learning-guided precipitation route is expected to be effective in multicomponent and refractory high-entropy alloys.
The route may not generalize across all alloy compositions and processing conditions.
